# Modeling hypertension prevalence: Logistic regression

## Background

We need to define a number of quantities.  Suppose a binary event occurs
with probability $p$, $0 \lt p \lt 1$.  We define the odds in favor of the event
as the quantity $p/(1-p)$.  Thus an event that occurs with probability 1/2
has "odds in favor" 1.0.  An event that occurs with probability 2/3 has odds
2:1 in favor.  The log odds is the natural log of the odds transformation
of the probability $p$.

We'll illustrate this concept with a simulation.  Recall
the definition of the Binomial distribution [here](https://vjcitn.github.io/2026vjc/slides/prob/20e-moments-models.html#the-binomial-distribution).  We'll
define
$$
Y_1, \ldots, Y_{100} \sim_{iid} \mbox{Bin}(1, 2/3)
$$
to be realized in a vector `y`.  We then use `glm`
to estimate the log odds in favor of $Y = 1$.
```{r lkbin}
set.seed(12345)
y = rbinom(100, 1, 2/3)
bmod = glm(y~1, data=data.frame(y=y), family="binomial")
summary(bmod)
phat = mean(y)
phat
oddsy = mean(y)/(1-mean(y))
oddsy
log(oddsy)
bmod$coef
```
We simulated a vector
of binary outcomes with success probability 2/3.  We work with the 
data and the fitted model in a few ways.

- The estimated success probability
is computed as $\hat{p} =~$`mean(y)`. 

- The odds in favor are
estimated directly as $\hat{p}/(1-\hat{p}) = `r oddsy`$.  

- The log of the odds in favor
is computed by `glm` as $\hat{\beta} = `r bmod$coef[1]`$, the sole coefficient estimate of `bmod`.

- We can recover $\hat{p}$ from the GLM fit by taking the "antilogit" of the estimated log 
odds: 
$$
\frac{\exp{\hat{\beta}}}{1+\exp{\hat{\beta}}} = `r plogis(bmod$coef[1])`
$$

Q7.  Use the NHANES data, filter to `SurveyYr` `2011_12`; call the resulting
data.frame `nh11`.

Define the binary response HTN as 1 if BPSysAve > 125 or BPDiaAve > 85, 0 otherwise.
If either component is missing, omit the observation.  

Here are two ways of visualizing prevalence of HTN in association with participant age.

```{r lkhtn,message=FALSE}
library(NHANES)
library(dplyr)
nh11 = NHANES |> filter(SurveyYr == "2011_12", !is.na(BPDiaAve))
nh11$HTN = 1*(nh11$BPSysAve > 125 | nh11$BPDiaAve > 85)
aged = cut(nh11$Age, c(-1,seq(10,85,10)))
ps = sapply(split(nh11$HTN, aged), mean, na.rm=TRUE)
logit = function(x) log(x/(1-x))
mpts = seq(5,84,10)
par(mfrow=c(1,2),las=2)
plot(ps~mpts, main="observed prevalence", xlab="age midpoints")
plot(logit(ps)~mpts, main="logit prevalence", xlab="age midpoints")
```
Notice that the y-values for data displayed on the left lie in (0,1).
In the display on the right, the logit transformation
"unconstrains" the vertical scale we use to plot the transformed prevalence statistics.

Notice further that on the logit scale, there is an approximately linear trajectory
in the estimated prevalences
as ages exceed 25 or so.  We will use this observation to motivate modeling
the prevalence of HTN across the adult ages with a lower bound of 25 years.
We use both a logistic regression with glm, and a linear regression.

Logistic:

```{r dom1}
m1 = glm(HTN~I(Age-50), data=nh11 |> filter(Age > 25), family="binomial")
m1nc = glm(HTN~Age, data=nh11 |> filter(Age > 25), family="binomial")
summary(m1)
```

Linear:

```{r thelin}
lm1 = lm(HTN~Age, data=nh11 |> filter(Age > 25))
summary(lm1)
```
We'll add the fitted lines to the summary scatterplots.

```{r dopl2}
par(mfrow=c(1,2),las=2)
plot(ps~mpts, main="observed prevalence", xlab="age midpoints")
abline(coef(lm1)[1], coef(lm1)[2], lty=2)
plot(logit(ps)~mpts, main="logit prevalence", xlab="age midpoints")
abline(coef(m1nc)[1], coef(m1nc)[2], lty=2)
```

a) What, according to the model `m1`, is the estimated probability of HTN for
a participant aged 50 years?  Remember that the parameters are obtained
on the logit scale.

b) Explain the relevance and approximate concordance of the following calculations.
Note that the `plogis` function computes, for argument x, `exp(x)/(1+exp(x))`.
```{r lkplo}
plogis(-.4621+20*0.04865)
mean(nh11$HTN[nh11$Age > 67.5 & nh11$Age < 72.5], na.rm=TRUE)
```

c) What is an approximate confidence interval for the log odds ratio
comparing risk of HTN for two individuals with an age difference of one year?
(To learn more about confidence intervals, be acquainted with [this](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/inference/estimates-confidence-intervals.html#confidence-intervals) and following
sections of the course textbook.)

d) Consider the following modified model: `m2 = update(m1, .~.*Sex)`.  What
does the `*` operator do?  What is a qualitative interpretation of the
coefficients of this model?

# Large sample theory

There are two facts that we appeal to in motivating and justifying
our interpretation of model estimates and confidence intervals.

## Law of large numbers

This law says that with sufficient sampling, the sample mean cannot take a value
differing very much from the "true mean".  Formally, for any
$\epsilon > 0$, for $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ independent with mean $\mu$ and finite variance,
$$
\mbox{Pr}(|\bar{X} - \mu|>\epsilon) \rightarrow 0 ~\mbox{as}~ n \rightarrow \infty.
$$


Q8.  In this code chunk, we use simulation of
data from a probability model with an asymmetric (positively skewed)
density: $\chi^2_3$.  
Note that some density traces are "clipped" at the top; expand the upper y boundary to see
the change in data concentration.  Note also that the density estimates have been scaled down
by a factor of 4 to improve visibility of the concentration process.

```{r dosimlln}
set.seed(1234)
x = seq(0,5,.1)
plot(x, dchisq(x,3), pch=".", col="blue", type="l", ylim=c(0,.4))
x5 = replicate(1000, mean(rchisq(5, 3)))
x50 = replicate(1000, mean(rchisq(50, 3)))
x150 = replicate(1000, mean(rchisq(150, 3)))
x500 = replicate(1000, mean(rchisq(500, 3)))
x5000 = replicate(1000, mean(rchisq(5000, 3)))
sdens = function(x,sc=4) {d = density(x); list(x=d$x, y=d$y/sc)}
lines(sdens(x5), lty=3)
lines(sdens(x50), lty=4)
lines(sdens(x150), lty=5, col="gold")
lines(sdens(x500), lty=6)
lines(sdens(x5000), lty=7, col="brown", lwd=1.5)
legend("topright", legend="N=150", col="gold", lty=5)
```

a. Describe in words how the various
traces of densities for the sample means for increasing
sample sizes illustrate the law of large numbers.

b. Improve the legend in this display by including
entries for all traces in the plot.

## Central limit theorem

In its simplest form, assuming
$X_1, \ldots, X_n$ independent with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$,
we have
$$
\sqrt{n}\left( \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma} \right) \rightarrow_d N(0,1)~\mbox{as}~n \rightarrow \infty
$$
We use $\rightarrow_d$ to denote "convergence in distribution", which you can learn
about in detail in a course on probability.  (When we estimate $\sigma$ and
use the sample standard deviation in the denominator, the convergence to
$N(0,1)$ is preserved.)

Here is a code chunk to illustrate one aspect of this form of convergence.
We are looking at the upper tail of the distribution of the t statistic 
for samples of varying sizes drawn from a distribution that is right-skewed.


```{r lkclt1}
set.seed(1234)
x = seq(-5,5,.05)
plot(x, dnorm(x), col="blue", type="l", lwd=2, xlim=c(1.5,4), ylim=c(-.01,.12))
tstat = function(x,truemean=3) {n = length(x); sqrt(n)*(mean(x)-truemean)/sd(x)}
R = 5000
x5 = replicate(R, tstat(rchisq(5, 3)))
x50 = replicate(R, tstat(rchisq(50, 3)))
x150 = replicate(R, tstat(rchisq(150, 3)))
x500 = replicate(R, tstat(rchisq(500, 3)))
x5000 = replicate(R, tstat(rchisq(5000, 3)))
lines(density(x5), lty=2,col="red")
lines(density(x50), lty=3,col="orange")
lines(density(x150), lty=4, col="gold")
lines(density(x500), lty=5,col="black")
lines(density(x5000), lty=6, col="brown", lwd=1.5)
legend("topright", lty=c(2:6), 
  legend=paste("N=", c(5,50,150,500,5000),sep=""), 
  col=c("red", "orange", "gold", "black", "brown"))
```
